content: 1. Degrees of prior exposure to Plasmodium falciparum were assessed using sporozoites administered via intramuscular injection. This study was published in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2014 (Volume 5, Article 686). 2. Spring M, Polhemus M, and Ockenhouse C conducted research on controlled human malaria infection, which was detailed in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2014 (Volume 209, Supplement 2, Pages S40–S45). 3. Hodgson SH, Juma E, Salim A, Magiri C, Njenga D, Molyneux S, and colleagues shared insights from the first controlled human malaria infection study conducted in Nairobi, Kenya. Their findings were published in the Malaria Journal in 2015 (Volume 14, Article 182). 4. Kilama WL explored ethical considerations in health research involving malaria vector trials in Africa, as documented in the Malaria Journal in 2010 (Volume 9, Supplement 3). 5. Andrade-Narvaez F, Canto-Lara SB, and Garcia-Miss MDR discussed ethical issues in entomological field studies on leishmaniasis in Developing World Bioethics in 2009 (Volume 9, Issue 3, Pages 157–160). 6. Achee NL, Youngblood L, Bangs MJ, Lavery JV, and James S provided a tool for investigators and regulators to consider the use of human participants in vector biology research. This was published in Vector-Borne and Zoonotic Diseases in 2015 (Volume 15, Issue 2, Pages 89–102). 7. Ndebele P and Musesengwa R addressed ethical dilemmas in malaria vector research in Africa, focusing on the challenges of balancing mosquito, science, and human interests. Their work appeared in the Malawi Medical Journal in 2012 (Volume 24, Pages 65–68). 8. Pereira Lima JB, Rosa-Freitas MG, Melo Rodovalho CM, Santos F, and Lourenço-de-Oliveira R reviewed the efficiency of traps and collection methods for sampling Anopheles darlingi and other malaria vectors. Their findings were published in Memórias do Instituto Oswaldo Cruz in 2014 (Volume 109, Issue 5, Pages 685–705). 9. The World Health Organization (WHO) provided information on malaria in pregnant women, accessible via their website as of July 15, 2020. 10. Friedman EE, Dallah F, Harville EW, Myers L, Buekens P, Breart G, and colleagues conducted a retrospective cohort study on symptomatic dengue infection during pregnancy and its impact on infant outcomes. This was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2014 (Volume 8, Issue 10, Article e3226). 11. WHO published key facts about the Zika virus, accessible via their website as of July 15, 2020. 12. Heyrana K, Byers HM, and Stratton P emphasized the importance of increasing the participation of pregnant women in clinical trials. Their commentary was published in JAMA in 2018 (Volume 320, Issue 20, Pages 2077–2078). 13. WHO developed a community engagement framework for quality, people-centered, and resilient health services, accessible via their website as of July 15, 2020. 14. WHO also provided a framework on integrated, people-centered health services, which was presented in the Sixty-ninth World Health Assembly in Geneva in 2016 and accessible online as of July 15, 2020. 15. Otmani del Barrio M examined the social dimensions of mosquito-borne diseases, their prevention, and control, with a focus on the Zika case in Latin America. This was included in the book Mosquitoes Management: Between Environmental and Health Issues, edited by Claeys C. 16. Selgelid MJ conducted an ethical analysis of gain-of-function research, which was published in Science and Engineering Ethics in 2016 (Volume 22, Issue 4, Pages 923–964). 17. WHO provided a module on community engagement (Module B5), accessible online as of July 15, 2020. 18. Kothari U and Cooke B discussed the concept of participation as a form of tyranny in their book Participation: The New Tyranny?, published by Zed Books in 2001. 19. Diabate A reported on the small-scale release of genetically modified sterile male mosquitoes in Bana, a village in Burkina Faso, as part of the Target Malaria initiative. This information was accessible online as of July 15, 2020. 20. Resnik DB explored ethical issues in field trials of genetically modified, disease-resistant mosquitoes in Developing World Bioethics in 2014 (Volume 14, Issue 1, Pages 37–46). 21. Beisel U and Ganle JK analyzed the release of genetically engineered mosquitoes in Burkina Faso, focusing on the bioeconomy of science, public engagement, and trust in medicine. Their work was published in the African Studies Review in 2019 (Volume 62, Issue 3, Pages 164–173). 22. Vector-borne diseases (VBDs) are significant contributors to global morbidity and mortality, disproportionately affecting the world’s poorest populations. Despite their growing burden, the ethical issues surrounding VBDs have received limited attention. Recognizing this gap, WHO developed guidance to assist programs and staff in identifying and addressing core ethical issues in VBD prevention and control. This guidance was created by an international group of experts in vector control, infectious disease ethics, maternal and child health, ecology, climate change, research, vaccine development, and public health communication. It examines a wide range of ethical considerations, including social and environmental determinants of health, vector control methods (including emerging technologies), screening, surveillance, research, vaccine campaigns, and mass drug administration. The guidance emphasizes the critical role of community engagement in designing and implementing sustainable public health responses.
